claims.text: The initial HEA is a homogeneous single-phase solid solution with clean grain boundaries and no significant segregation or intermetallic phases.
Thermal and mechanical loading triggers diffusion and preferential segregation of alloying elements to grain boundaries.
Cr, Mn, and Ni are minor alloying elements in the proposed HEA.
Elevated-temperature segregation produces nanoscale Cr-, Ni-, or Mn-enriched zones at high-angle grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation and nanoclustering reduce grain-boundary cohesive strength.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion promotes crack initiation and localized brittle intergranular failure.
Localized grain-boundary enrichment can cause failure while the bulk alloy remains a single-phase solid solution.
Conventional-alloy embrittlement is primarily caused by extensive grain-boundary precipitation rather than incipient segregation.
Thermal cycling around 700°C combined with high-strain-rate or shear loading is an appropriate intervention for testing the proposed mechanism.
The applicable temperature range activates grain-boundary diffusion without causing bulk phase separation or macroscopic second-phase precipitation.
Progressive loading will cause the onset and growth of nanoscale grain-boundary compositional heterogeneities.
The emergence of grain-boundary nanoclusters will correlate with a transition from ductile, strain-hardened deformation to brittle fracture.
The predicted ductile-to-brittle trend will be less pronounced or differently manifested in conventional alloys.
The hypothesis is restricted to moderate-temperature, mechanically loaded service before prolonged exposure produces macroscopic precipitation.
Trace impurities and interstitial elements may alter segregation or phase-separation behavior.
The segregation kinetics and critical grain-boundary concentration for embrittlement are unknown.
Absence of significant grain-boundary enrichment or absence of a correlation between enrichment and brittle fracture would falsify the hypothesis.
